title: Kedoshim: don't stand idly by (Leviticus 19:16)
hook: "neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbor"

segments.voice: Yesterday in Kedoshim, no stumbling block before the blind. Your line was no stumbling blocks. Today, a verse that won't let anyone just watch, and the end of a week.

A person falls on a busy train platform. Plenty of people see it, and each one waits, half-sure somebody else will step forward. Someone is being piled on in a group chat, and the messages get read, one by one, and nobody types a thing. Psychologists call this kind of waiting the bystander effect. Leviticus 19 put the problem into a single verse, long before anyone gave it a name.
screen: `A FALL ON A BUSY PLATFORM.` → `EVERYONE WAITS FOR SOMEONE.` → `ONE VERSE, LONG BEFORE.`

segments.voice: The verse, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people; neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour: I am the LORD." Notice the pairing: don't spread stories, and don't stay out of it. Talk too much, or do too little: both fail a neighbor. Literally, the Hebrew says: do not stand upon your neighbor's blood. Standing still while someone bleeds. The translators added idly, and it fits. The Talmud asks where we learn that if you see someone drowning, or dragged off by a wild animal, or attacked by robbers, you are obligated to save them. The answer: from this verse. And it goes further: if you can't save them yourself, you must hire others to help. Maimonides rules that anyone who could save a life and doesn't has broken this commandment. Being present and doing nothing is not neutral. Look back at the week. Azazel carried the wrongs away. Ask the person first. Live by them. Then Kedoshim: holiness for everyone, the corners of the field, no stumbling block, and now this. The Kedoshim days each hand an ordinary person a job. Not the priest. You, on the platform, in the group chat, at the scene.
screen: `NO TALEBEARING, NO STANDING BY.` · `DON'T STAND UPON HIS BLOOD.` · `DROWNING, BEASTS, ROBBERS.` · `A WEEK OF ORDINARY JOBS.` · then, large: `DON'T STAND IDLY BY.`

segments.voice: Think of a place where you've been a bystander lately: a coworker everyone talks over, a neighbor who seems to be struggling, a thread where someone's getting piled on. Picture yourself being the one who does something. Not heroic: a question, a call, a message, a word in a meeting.
Kedoshim. The portion that says you may not stand idly by your neighbor's blood: if you can help, you must.
Your line: don't stand idly by. Watching is never quite neutral. Another week of Leviticus, done.

howItsDone: Jewish law treats rescuing someone in danger as a positive duty, drawn from Leviticus 19:16, and the verse is often cited in Jewish teaching about speaking up for people in danger or being harmed.
